prompt: I'm a staff engineer at Northwind Payments. Our billing service is about 180,000 lines of code written in an older language whose runtime loses vendor support in March 2027. I want to propose rewriting it in the compiled language our ledger team adopted last year. The plan uses 5 engineers for 9 months, then runs the old and new services side by side for 6 weeks before cutover. I'm assuming the ledger team's experience means we won't need to hire from outside. What I don't know is how many undocumented edge cases are in the proration and refund logic. Nobody who wrote that code still works here. I have 20 minutes with our CTO, Dana Okafor, on November 4. Please find the holes in this plan the way she would. Then tell me which weaknesses I should fix before the meeting and which I should just acknowledge openly while I'm in the room.

I'm a product manager at Acme Forms, a paid online form builder. Our plans start at $29 a month and we have about 4,200 paying customers. Today we offer a 14-day trial, and 11 percent of trial users convert to paid. I want to propose a permanent free tier capped at 3 forms and 100 submissions a month. The goal is more top-of-funnel signups and word of mouth. My key assumption is that at least 4 percent of free users will upgrade within 6 months. I don't yet know what each free user will cost us in support and hosting, and I'm not sure whether some current customers on the cheapest plan would downgrade. I'm presenting this to our founder, Ravi Mehta, and our VP of Revenue, Claire Dubois, in two weeks. Please give me the objections they are most likely to raise, ranked by how damaging each would be. For each one, tell me what data I'd need to bring to answer it.

I lead a team of 14 engineers at Bluefin Logistics. We ship on a fixed release train every second Thursday, and each train carries about 40 merged changes. Last quarter we had 2 full rollbacks, and both took most of a day because we couldn't tell which change caused the problem. I want to propose moving to continuous deploys, where every change ships on its own once it passes checks, with the switch completed by the end of Q1 2027. I'm assuming our current automated tests, at roughly 68 percent coverage, catch enough regressions to make this safe. An open question is how customer success will cope, since they currently publish release notes for each train and brief support staff beforehand. This is going to our Director of Engineering, Priya Nair, who signed off on the release train process three years ago. Please stress-test the proposal and list the questions she is likely to ask. Keep the output short enough that I can turn it into a one-page brief.

I'm a data engineer at Harbor Outfitters, a mid-sized retail company. Leadership wants an internal analytics dashboard for sales, inventory and margin. A vendor has quoted us $96,000 a year for 60 seats. I'm proposing that we build it ourselves instead. My estimate is 2 engineers for 4 months, plus about a quarter of one engineer's time ongoing for maintenance. I'm assuming our needs stay at roughly 25 standard reports that change a few times a year. The unknown is whether finance will want self-serve ad hoc querying next year. If they do, the build effort grows considerably. I also haven't priced the hosting and access control work carefully. The decision belongs to our CFO, Marcus Lee, who is skeptical of internal tools after a past project ran over. Please give me an honest comparison of build versus buy that shows where my build case is weakest. Then tell me what Marcus will most likely push back on.

I'm a product manager at Tidepool, a meal-planning service that is web-only today. We have about 310,000 monthly active users, and 72 percent of sessions come from mobile browsers. I want to propose native apps for both major phone platforms, built by a team of 4 over 6 months, with launch targeted for June 2027. My central assumption is that app users will retain about 1.5 times better than mobile web users, based on what a competitor said at a conference. One open question is how app store fees would affect our margins, since around 18 percent of new subscriptions start on mobile. I also haven't decided whether the apps launch with full feature parity or a subset. I'm presenting this to our CEO and co-founder, Elena Park, at the planning review on December 9. Please tell me the three questions she is most likely to ask. Also tell me where my numbers are too thin to survive a challenge.

I manage a site reliability team of 10 at Quillstack. Six of us are in Lisbon and four are in Denver. Right now one person is primary on-call for a full week at a time. Over the last quarter we averaged 23 pages a week, 9 of them overnight for whoever was on call, and two people have told me they are close to burning out. I want to propose a follow-the-sun rotation where each site covers its own daytime in shifts of about 12 hours. I'm assuming the Denver group can sustain their half of the rotation with only 4 people. What I haven't worked out is whether the 7-hour time difference leaves coverage gaps or awkward handoffs, or how the on-call stipend should change. This goes to our VP of Infrastructure, Tom Reyes, next month. Please stress-test the proposal, especially on fairness and coverage gaps. Give me a short list of risks, each with a mitigation I could propose alongside it.

I'm an engineering manager at Corvid Software, which has 220 engineers. I want to propose rolling out Scribe, an AI code assistant from a vendor called Lanternworks, to every engineer starting January 5, 2027, at $39 per seat per month. We ran a 6-week pilot with 25 engineers, and participants reported finishing pull requests about 20 percent faster. Those numbers are self-reported, not measured. I'm assuming the pilot results will hold across all our teams, including the embedded firmware group, which didn't take part. Our legal team hasn't yet reviewed whether code sent to the vendor is retained or used for training, and I don't know how long that review will take. The proposal will be reviewed jointly by our CTO, Aisha Bello, and our General Counsel, Henrik Sand. Please give me the toughest objections each of them is likely to raise. Then tell me what evidence I'm missing that would make the proposal hold up.

I'm head of product at Meridian Payroll. Our draft roadmap for Q1 2027 has 7 initiatives spread across 30 engineers, and in my view none of them will be done well. I want to propose cutting it to two bets: multi-state tax filing and a mobile timesheet app. My assumption is that dropping the other five won't cost us renewals. However, 3 of the dropped items were discussed with enterprise customers who together represent about $1.2 million in annual recurring revenue. The open question is whether sales made written commitments to any of those customers, or only verbal ones. I haven't been able to confirm either way. I'm presenting at the leadership offsite on November 12 to our CEO, Jordan Wells, and the rest of the executive team. Please argue against my proposal as our Chief Revenue Officer would. Then tell me which of those arguments I have no good answer to yet.

I'm the platform lead at Stratus Maps. Version 1 of our public API still handles about 6 percent of traffic, and keeping it running costs us roughly 1.5 engineers' worth of effort. Most of the remaining traffic comes from 5 large customers, and one of them pays us around $400,000 a year. My plan is to announce deprecation on December 1, 2026 and shut version 1 off on June 30, 2027. I'm assuming each of those customers can migrate within 6 months using our migration guide and some help from our solutions engineers. The unknown is one customer that may have version 1 calls embedded in hardware devices already deployed in the field, which they might not be able to update remotely. I'm taking this to our COO, Hana Kimura, who owns the customer relationships. Please point out the weaknesses in the plan. Also tell me what I should ask our account managers before the meeting.

I lead developer relations at Kestrel, a command-line developer tool with about 48,000 weekly active developers. I'm proposing that we launch a public changelog and a community forum in February 2027. That means hiring one community manager at roughly $110,000 a year and setting aside about 10 percent of engineering time for answering forum threads. I'm assuming the forum will reduce our support tickets, currently about 900 a month, by 15 percent within two quarters. Two things are unknown. I don't know what the moderation load will be, and I don't know whether a detailed public changelog would reveal our direction to Brightline, our closest competitor. Our founder and owner, Sam Achebe, has to approve the hire and has said before that forums tend to become ghost towns. Please give me a list of the risks in this proposal. Then give me a blunt read on whether it's ready to take to Sam or needs more work first.
